articles.title: Same-day test helps doctors detect hidden infections in critically ill children
articles.summary: Metagenomics offers a new way of detecting infections in intensive care patients.
articles.content:
"The fact that they had a test there available to her was paramount. It saved her life," said Stacey.

"It's a miracle she's here and we're extremely grateful for that," added Willow's dad, Russ.

With the right treatment, Willow was eventually able to recover from her infection, but needed several months in hospital.

She is one of many patients at the children's hospital to benefit from the new type of testing.

During a study in 2024-5 metagenomic testing was used on 122 critically ill children in the paediatric intensive care unit (ICU) at GOSH.

The results have now been published in the Lancet Microbe.

Metagenomic testing analyses all genetic material in a sample and can detect thousands of different pathogens.

By contrast, the most common method of identifying bacteria is by trying to culture them in Petri dishes, a technology that has been used since Victorian times.

Another test, PCR, can identify viruses and some bacteria, but doctors need to specify what they are trying to detect.

Metagenomics testing at GOSH was able to identify around nine in 10 bacteria and viruses and all fungi in samples.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant medical breakthrough in detecting infections in critically ill children using metagenomic testing, which has a broad and meaningful impact on patient outcomes in pediatric intensive care. The testing method improves upon traditional techniques by identifying a wide range of pathogens quickly, enabling timely and effective treatment that can save lives. The story includes concrete data from a study and real patient impact, fulfilling criteria for inspiring good news.
articles.personality_title: New same-day test quickly finds hidden infections in critically ill children
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Detecting infections in very sick children is often difficult because traditional tests can take days or only find certain germs. Doctors need faster and better ways to find out what is making a child sick so they can give the right treatment quickly.

**What happened** – At Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH) in London, doctors used a new test called metagenomic testing on 122 children in the pediatric intensive care unit during 2024-2025. This test looks at all the genetic material in a sample, which helps find many types of bacteria, viruses, and fungi at once. The study results were published in the medical journal Lancet Microbe.

**Impact** – This new test found about 90% of bacteria and viruses and all fungi in the samples, much more than traditional methods. For example, Willow, a young patient, had a hidden infection that only this test could find quickly. Thanks to the test, doctors could treat her in time, saving her life and helping her recover after months in the hospital.

**What’s next step** – Hospitals may start using metagenomic testing more often to check very sick children faster and more accurately. This could help doctors give the right medicines sooner and improve the chances of recovery for many patients.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new same-day metagenomic test helps doctors find hidden infections quickly in very sick children, leading to faster treatment and better outcomes.

**Impact** – Ce nouveau test a détecté environ 90 % des bactéries et virus et tous les champignons présents, bien plus que les méthodes traditionnelles. articles.title: A fungus is threatening the world’s food supply. Scientists just found a new defense
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a potential new weapon against a devastating fungus that threatens rice, wheat, and barley worldwide. By engineering a special type of plant immune receptor, researchers created defenses capable of recognizing multiple fungal threats at once. The breakthrough could eventually lead to crops with powerful, long-lasting disease resistance, helping protect a global food supply increasingly threatened by spreading infections and climate change.
articles.content:
Scientists have uncovered a promising new way to protect some of the world's most important food crops from a destructive fungus that threatens global food security. By engineering the natural immune defenses of plants, researchers have developed an experimental approach that could eventually help wheat, rice, and barley resist fungal infections more effectively.

The international research team, led by scientists at the John Innes Centre in the United Kingdom, investigated a recently discovered group of plant immune receptors. They identified how these proteins recognize invading pathogens and demonstrated that they can be modified to detect multiple fungal threats. The findings could open the door to crops with stronger, more durable disease resistance.

"We've discovered something that could lead to a potential intervention on what is the worst fungal disease of cereals," said Professor Mark Banfield, a research group leader at the John Innes Centre and an author of the study, which involved collaborators at Kobe University in Japan.

A Devastating Fungus Threatens the Global Food Supply

The target of the research is Magnaporthe oryzae, the fungus responsible for blast disease. It causes the most serious fungal disease affecting cultivated rice and has also become a major threat to wheat and barley in parts of Asia and Africa.

The damage is enormous. Each year, rice blast destroys enough rice to feed approximately 60 million people. As the fungus spreads into additional agricultural regions, developing effective ways to protect crops has become increasingly important for global food security.

The fungus infects plants through a sophisticated biological strategy. It delivers specialized molecules known as effectors into cells in the leaves and stems. These molecules interfere with normal plant functions, allowing the pathogen to establish an infection and promote disease.

Plants, however, have evolved their own defense systems. Specialized immune receptors can recognize these foreign molecules and trigger a protective response. One important mechanism involves causing infected cells to die in a controlled, localized area, helping prevent the pathogen from spreading farther through the plant.

Scientists Discover a Hidden Plant Immune Defense

For more than three decades, much of the research into plant immunity has centered on proteins called Nucleotide-binding and leucine-rich receptors (NLRs). These receptors have played a central role in understanding how crops recognize and defend themselves against blast disease and other infections.

More recently, scientists have begun investigating another group of immune proteins found in cereal crops, known as tandem kinase proteins (TKPs). Although researchers are still learning how these receptors operate, they appear to offer additional opportunities for strengthening plant defenses.

Earlier studies revealed that some TKPs contain a specialized region called a Heavy Metal Associated (HMA) domain. Similar regions are also found in certain NLR receptors, where they help recognize pathogen effectors and initiate immune responses.

This shared feature attracted the attention of Banfield and his colleagues because it suggested that scientists might be able to redesign the receptors to recognize additional fungal threats.

"This piqued our interest," said Professor Banfield. "If we can engineer these integrated HMA domains for new properties by making amino acid protein changes where effectors bind, we can gain what we call novel recognition specificities - and potentially a new frontline for defense of plants against disease."

Turning Fungal Attack Molecules Into Targets

In the study, published in Science Advances, researchers examined precisely how HMA domains interact with the molecules released by the blast fungus.

Using biophysical techniques and crystallography, a method that allows scientists to determine the detailed three-dimensional structure of molecules, the team obtained a high-resolution view of how these plant receptors bind to fungal effectors.

The results revealed that HMA domains can function as biological bait. By binding to molecules the fungus uses during infection, these regions help plants recognize the presence of an invading pathogen and activate their defenses.

Armed with this structural information, the researchers modified TKP immune receptors so they could recognize two different fungal effectors associated with infections in wheat and barley.

This ability to detect multiple targets, known as dual specificity, is unusual in naturally occurring immune receptors. Demonstrating that it can be introduced through protein engineering suggests a promising way to expand the range of threats that crop immune systems can recognize.

The findings also provide a foundation for investigating other recently identified TKPs in different cereal crops. Scientists may eventually be able to design customized immune receptors that detect several fungal effectors simultaneously, potentially making plants more difficult for pathogens to infect.

Engineering Crops With Stronger Disease Resistance

Although the findings are encouraging, the technology remains at an early experimental stage.

The researchers conducted their initial tests using protoplasts, individual wheat cells that serve as a simplified model for studying how plant tissues respond. The next step is to determine whether the engineered receptors can provide effective protection in whole plants grown under controlled greenhouse conditions.

"Our study indicates that this new class of resistance proteins is amenable for engineering purposes. We now know that the previous tools we used in engineering NLR receptors may also work with this new class," said Dr. Daniel Yu, the first author of the study.

Understanding exactly how fungal effectors attach to plant immune receptors could also help researchers take advantage of other technologies. Precision breeding and artificial intelligence may provide additional ways to redesign HMA domains, allowing them to recognize pathogen molecules that previously escaped detection.

One particularly promising possibility involves combining different types of immune receptors within the same crop.

Because NLRs and TKPs appear to activate plant defenses through different mechanisms, using them together could create several layers of protection. This might make it harder for fungi to evolve ways around a plant's immune system.

"We think these two classes of immune receptors, NLRs and TKPs, are probably activated in different ways," said Professor Banfield. "That gives the potential for more robust immunity in the field because you are not putting all your eggs in one basket. Further down the road, we may be able to use techniques to stack genes encoding TKPs and NLRs together against the same disease, making a super-resistant crop. They will have different ways of activating immunity, so it is likely to be more difficult for a pathogen to evolve away from," he added.

A Growing Threat to Wheat, Rice, and Barley

The need for better protection is becoming more urgent as blast disease continues to threaten major food crops.

Wheat blast was first identified in Brazil during the 1980s and has since spread to parts of Asia and Africa. Although the disease has not been detected in the United Kingdom, climate change could eventually create conditions that allow it to threaten cereal production in northern Europe.

For farmers, the emergence of blast disease in new regions presents a serious challenge, particularly because the fungus can threaten crops that are essential to feeding large populations.

By revealing how a previously underexplored class of plant immune receptors can be engineered to recognize multiple fungal threats, the researchers have identified a possible new strategy for protecting future harvests.

Further testing will be necessary to establish whether these modified defenses work effectively in whole plants and under agricultural conditions. If successful, combining different immune receptors could eventually help scientists develop crops with more resilient protection against one of agriculture's most destructive fungal diseases.

This advancement has broad implications for improving crop resilience, combating food insecurity, and addressing challenges posed by climate change. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights a meaningful positive impact on society.

articles.title: Rare study reveals a striking divide inside an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain
articles.summary: A rare examination of an Alzheimer’s patient’s brain revealed that regions cleared of amyloid plaques had remarkably little of the harmful tau buildup associated with memory loss, while neighboring areas showed extensive damage. The discovery suggests that removing amyloid may have lasting protective effects and could help slow Alzheimer’s progression, especially when treatment begins early.
articles.content:
An unusually detailed examination of an Alzheimer's patient's brain has revealed striking differences between regions where treatment successfully removed harmful amyloid plaques and areas where those plaques remained. The regions cleared of amyloid showed little or no buildup of tau tangles, another protein abnormality strongly associated with brain cell damage and declining memory. Nearby areas that still contained amyloid, however, showed much higher levels of tau and evidence of continued neurodegeneration.

The discovery offers rare evidence from a human brain that removing amyloid plaques may provide protection against other damaging processes involved in Alzheimer's disease (AD). The results also suggest that clearing amyloid thoroughly, particularly early in the disease, could help limit tau accumulation and slow the progression of brain damage.

Researchers from the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania presented the findings at the 2026 Alzheimer's Association International Conference. The study was also published in JAMA.

"Seeing both disease patterns side-by-side in the same brain gave us a rare opportunity to understand how amyloid removal affects other proteins that contribute to Alzheimer's disease," said co-senior author David Wolk, MD, co-director of the Penn Memory Center and director of the Penn Alzheimer's Disease Research Center. "The findings provide some of the clearest human evidence to date that anti-amyloid therapies may limit the accumulation of tau and slow the brain changes that lead to memory loss and cognitive decline."

How Amyloid and Tau Contribute to Alzheimer's Disease

Two proteins play major roles in the development of Alzheimer's disease. Beta-amyloid collects outside nerve cells, forming sticky deposits known as plaques. Tau, meanwhile, accumulates inside neurons and forms abnormal tangles. Both are associated with the progressive damage to brain cells that contributes to memory problems, changes in personality, and difficulties with thinking.

Treatments designed to eliminate amyloid plaques have significantly changed how Alzheimer's is managed in recent years. Aducanumab became the first drug of this type to receive accelerated approval from the FDA, although it is no longer sold. Since then, newer and more effective medications that target amyloid through a similar approach, donanemab (Kisunla) and lecanemab (Leqembi), have received full FDA approval.

Researchers have long believed that amyloid buildup helps create the conditions in which harmful tau tangles develop. What has been much harder to establish is whether eliminating amyloid can also limit tau accumulation in the human brain.

Direct evidence has been scarce because relatively few people who received amyloid-clearing drugs have undergone brain examinations after death.

A Rare Brain Examination Reveals a Striking Pattern

The researchers were able to investigate this question using brain tissue donated by a former Alzheimer's clinical trial participant.

The man was in his fifties when he was diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment caused by Alzheimer's disease. He subsequently joined a clinical trial testing aducanumab and received 30 doses of the medication over four and a half years.

He died approximately four years after his last dose, more than a decade after his first symptoms appeared. Before his death, he expressed a wish to donate his brain to scientific research. The tissue was provided to the Center for Neurodegenerative Disease Research in the Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine.

When specialists examined the donated brain, they discovered an unusual pattern in which neighboring regions showed dramatically different amounts of Alzheimer's-related damage.

The raised ridges of the brain's folded surface, known as gyri, had lost most of their amyloid plaques and contained very little accumulated tau. In contrast, the neighboring grooves between these ridges, called sulci, still contained considerable amyloid buildup. These regions also exhibited substantially more tau tangles, inflammation, and degeneration of brain tissue.

This patchwork distribution was consistent with scans taken while the patient was alive, which had already indicated that amyloid removal varied considerably across different parts of his brain.

"Many previous reports have shown either extensive amyloid clearance or limited clearance," said co-senior author Edward B. Lee, MD, PhD, the John Q. Trojanowski, MD, PhD Professor for Neurodegenerative Disease Research in Pathology and Laboratory Medicine. "This case represented a unique 'Goldilocks' scenario in which some regions cleared amyloid and others did not. It allowed us to directly compare what happened next in neighboring brain regions and better understand the relationship between amyloid, tau, and neurodegeneration."

Could Alzheimer's Treatments Protect the Brain for Years?

The findings could have important implications for the latest generation of Alzheimer's medications, which remove amyloid using mechanisms similar to the therapy received by this patient.

Although the investigation involved only one individual, the contrast between different brain regions suggests that substantial amyloid removal may influence other disease processes long after treatment has stopped.

The results also raise an important question about how the benefits of Alzheimer's drugs are measured. Clinical trials commonly evaluate patients over approximately 18 months, but some protective effects might take considerably longer to become apparent.

However, the study cannot establish how much amyloid must be removed to achieve lasting protection or prove that plaque clearance was directly responsible for the differences in tau accumulation and brain damage.

Researchers now hope to understand why certain parts of the brain respond more effectively to amyloid-clearing treatments than others. Identifying and potentially strengthening the biological mechanisms responsible for plaque removal could lead to better therapies.

Another major question is whether beginning treatment before extensive tau tangles develop could substantially delay Alzheimer's or even prevent the disease from emerging.

Why Earlier Alzheimer's Treatment Could Matter

Because amyloid can accumulate silently in the brain for many years before memory problems begin, researchers are increasingly interested in treating people during the earliest stages of the disease, potentially before noticeable symptoms appear.

"Patients may accumulate amyloid for years before symptoms appear," said first author Christopher A. Brown, MD, PhD, an assistant professor of Neurology. "This case suggests that removing amyloid early may help limit the changes that ultimately damage brain cells. Ongoing trials will help determine whether starting treatment before symptoms begin can provide even greater benefit."

This research received support from the National Institutes of Health (P30-AG072979, RF1-AG069474, R01-AG056014, R01-AG055005, R01-AG072796, R01-AG065341, P01-AG084497).
articles.reasoning: The article reports a rare and detailed human brain study that provides important evidence that removing amyloid plaques may protect against tau buildup and neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's disease. This finding has broad significance for Alzheimer's treatment strategies and could lead to improved therapies that slow or prevent disease progression, benefiting many people worldwide. The article is focused, detailed, and highlights a meaningful scientific breakthrough with tangible health impacts.
articles.personality_title: Study shows clearing amyloid plaques may protect brain in Alzheimer’s disease
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Alzheimer’s disease harms the brain by building up two harmful proteins: amyloid plaques outside brain cells and tau tangles inside them. These proteins damage brain cells and cause memory loss and thinking problems. Some new medicines try to remove amyloid plaques to slow the disease.

After he died, scientists examined his brain and found that areas where amyloid plaques were removed had very little tau buildup. But nearby areas that still had amyloid showed a lot of tau and brain damage.

**Impact** – This is one of the clearest examples from a human brain that removing amyloid plaques might protect the brain by also stopping tau from building up. It suggests that treatments removing amyloid could slow down Alzheimer’s damage, especially if started early. The study also shows that different parts of the brain can respond differently to treatment.

**What’s next step** – Scientists want to learn why some brain areas clear amyloid better than others and how much amyloid must be removed for long-term benefits. They also plan to study if starting treatment before symptoms appear can prevent or delay Alzheimer’s.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Removing amyloid plaques in the brain may help stop harmful tau buildup and slow Alzheimer’s disease progression, especially when treatment starts early.

articles.personality_presentation_fr:

Mais les zones voisines avec encore des plaques amyloïdes présentaient beaucoup de tau et de dommages cérébraux.

articles.personality_title_es: Estudio muestra que eliminar placas amiloides puede proteger el cerebro en Alzheimer
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La enfermedad de Alzheimer daña el cerebro al acumular dos proteínas dañinas: placas amiloides fuera de las células cerebrales y ovillos de tau dentro. Estas proteínas dañan las células cerebrales y causan pérdida de memoria y problemas para pensar. Algunos medicamentos nuevos intentan eliminar las placas amiloides para frenar la enfermedad.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores estudiaron el cerebro de un hombre con Alzheimer que recibió un medicamento llamado aducanumab para eliminar placas amiloides. Tras su muerte, encontraron que las áreas donde se eliminaron las placas tenían muy poca acumulación de tau. Pero las zonas cercanas que aún tenían placas mostraban mucho tau y daño cerebral.

**Impacto** – Este es uno de los ejemplos más claros en un cerebro humano que muestra que eliminar placas amiloides puede proteger el cerebro al evitar también que se acumule tau. Sugiere que estos tratamientos podrían ralentizar el daño de Alzheimer, especialmente si se comienzan temprano. El estudio también muestra que diferentes partes del cerebro responden distinto al tratamiento.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos quieren entender por qué algunas áreas del cerebro eliminan mejor las placas y cuánto hay que eliminar para obtener beneficios duraderos. También estudiarán si comenzar el tratamiento antes de que aparezcan los síntomas puede prevenir o retrasar Alzheimer.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Eliminar las placas amiloides en el cerebro puede ayudar a detener la acumulación dañina de tau y frenar el avance del Alzheimer, especialmente si el tratamiento empieza temprano.

articles.title: Probiotic cuts risk of respiratory infections in formula-fed babies
articles.summary: Babies who are formula fed are more prone to infections, but the addition of a probiotic supplement containing sugars from breast milk slashed the risk of such infants catching respiratory viruses
articles.content:
Babies who are formula fed are more prone to infections, but the addition of a probiotic supplement containing sugars from breast milk slashed the risk of such infants catching respiratory viruses

Formula-fed babies may benefit from a probiotic, however, further research is needed damircudic/Getty Images

Adding a probiotic supplement to formula milk slashed rates of respiratory infections in babies who weren’t breastfed. Infections are more common in formula-fed babies, but the supplement – which contained both sugars from breast milk and the bacteria needed to ferment them – produced fatty molecules that seemed to strengthen the infants’ immune systems. This helped them eliminate viruses that cause symptoms like sneezing and a runny nose.

“It’s phenomenally exciting,” says Daniel Davis at Imperial College London, who wasn’t involved in the research. A high burden of early-life infections has been linked to more moderate to severe infections in later life and an increased risk of allergies. “Modifying formula milk to help set up good immune health for babies is a really powerful concept,” says Davis.

However, such interventions could have unintended consequences, including actually increasing the risk of allergies. “If you increase the power of someone’s immune response against infections, that might make them more likely to be susceptible to allergies or autoimmunity,” says Davis, who learned about the supplement at the Immunology of the Exposome conference at the Royal Society in London on 12 October. “These interventions are likely to have both pros and cons; we don’t know what those all are yet.”

Advertisement

Prior trials suggest that supplements containing sugars from breast milk, called human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs), cut rates of respiratory infections in such infants. These sugars are fermented by gut bacteria, including Bifidobacterium longum infantis, to produce short-chain fatty acids, molecules that seem to enhance immune responses against pathogens like viruses and bacteria.

But some babies, especially those in Western nations, lack B. longum infantis in their guts, which may be related to their mother’s diet. Previously, Petter Brodin at Imperial College London and his colleagues found that supplements that boost levels of this bacterium seemed to improve immune health in breast-fed babies.

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

Now, Brodin’s team has developed a supplement containing both HMOs and B. longum infantis and tested it on formula-fed babies, who are more likely to lack B. longum infantis.

With funding from Nestlé, which develops formula milk, the researchers recruited 223 infants – aged between 2 and 5 weeks – who were exclusively formula fed in Manila, the Philippines. About half of the infants were randomly assigned to drink formula milk made from a powder containing the probiotic supplement, while the remaining infants consumed the same milk without the supplement.

The parents – who were blinded as to which group their baby was in – logged whenever they showed symptoms of respiratory infections, such as sneezing, coughing or a runny nose, until they were 6 months old.

During this time, 23 per cent of the infants in the supplement group were recorded as developing an infection, compared with 40 per cent in the formula-only group. The former infants also recovered a few days faster from the infections, on average. “The respiratory infections were fewer and their duration was shorter,” says Brodin.

Further analysis of stool samples revealed that the supplement seems to boost levels of B. longum infantis in the gut, while reducing inflammation and supporting immune responses against pathogens.

The researchers need to carry out large trials that track the supplement’s effects in different countries over time, says Davis. Brodin says the team is planning to explore how it affects the risk of allergies and asthma.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant health breakthrough where a probiotic supplement added to formula milk substantially reduces respiratory infections in formula-fed infants, a group at higher risk. The study involved a well-defined trial with measurable positive outcomes, indicating broad potential benefits for infant health worldwide. While further research is needed, the current findings offer hopeful implications for improving immune health in a vulnerable population.
articles.personality_title: Probiotic supplement reduces respiratory infections in formula-fed babies
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Babies who are fed with formula milk instead of breast milk tend to get more respiratory infections, like colds or runny noses. This is because breast milk contains special sugars and bacteria that help protect babies from viruses.

**What happened** – Scientists added a probiotic supplement to formula milk. This supplement had sugars found in breast milk and a helpful type of bacteria called Bifidobacterium longum infantis. They tested it on 223 formula-fed babies in the Philippines, aged 2 to 5 weeks. Half the babies got formula with the supplement, and the other half got regular formula. The parents recorded if their babies had respiratory infections until they were 6 months old.

**Impact** – The babies who drank the supplemented formula had fewer infections—23% got sick compared to 40% of babies who drank regular formula. They also got better faster. The supplement helped increase the good bacteria in their guts and made their immune systems stronger. This is important because it shows a way to help protect babies who cannot be breastfed.

**What’s next step** – Researchers want to do bigger studies in different countries to see if the supplement works the same way everywhere. They also plan to check if the supplement affects allergies or asthma later in childhood.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Adding a probiotic supplement with breast milk sugars to formula milk helps protect formula-fed babies from respiratory infections and supports their immune health.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un complément probiotique réduit les infections respiratoires chez les bébés nourris au lait infantile
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les bébés nourris au lait infantile ont plus souvent des infections respiratoires, comme le rhume ou le nez qui coule, car le lait maternel contient des sucres et des bactéries qui les protègent.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des scientifiques ont ajouté un complément probiotique au lait infantile. Ce complément contenait des sucres du lait maternel et une bactérie bénéfique appelée Bifidobacterium longum infantis. Ils ont testé ce complément sur 223 bébés nourris exclusivement au lait infantile aux Philippines, âgés de 2 à 5 semaines. La moitié des bébés ont reçu du lait avec le complément, l’autre moitié du lait normal. Les parents ont noté les infections respiratoires jusqu’à ce que les bébés aient 6 mois.

**Impact** – Les bébés qui ont bu le lait avec le complément ont eu moins d’infections : 23 % ont été malades contre 40 % dans le groupe sans complément. Ils ont aussi guéri plus vite. Le complément a aidé à augmenter les bonnes bactéries dans leur intestin et à renforcer leur système immunitaire. Cela montre une nouvelle façon de protéger les bébés qui ne peuvent pas être allaités.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent faire de plus grandes études dans d’autres pays pour vérifier si le complément fonctionne partout. Ils veulent aussi voir s’il influence les allergies ou l’asthme plus tard.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Ajouter un complément probiotique avec des sucres du lait maternel au lait infantile aide à protéger les bébés nourris au lait infantile contre les infections respiratoires et soutient leur santé immunitaire.
articles.personality_title_es: Un suplemento probiótico reduce las infecciones respiratorias en bebés alimentados con fórmula
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los bebés que se alimentan con leche de fórmula tienen más infecciones respiratorias, como resfriados o mocos, porque la leche materna contiene azúcares y bacterias que los protegen.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos añadieron un suplemento probiótico a la leche de fórmula. Este suplemento tenía azúcares de la leche materna y una bacteria beneficiosa llamada Bifidobacterium longum infantis. Lo probaron en 223 bebés alimentados solo con fórmula en Filipinas, de 2 a 5 semanas de edad. A la mitad les dieron fórmula con el suplemento y a la otra mitad fórmula normal. Los padres anotaron si sus bebés tenían infecciones respiratorias hasta los 6 meses.

**Impacto** – Los bebés que tomaron la fórmula con el suplemento tuvieron menos infecciones: el 23 % se enfermó frente al 40 % de los que tomaron fórmula normal. También se recuperaron más rápido. El suplemento ayudó a aumentar las bacterias buenas en sus intestinos y fortaleció su sistema inmunológico. Esto es importante porque muestra cómo ayudar a proteger a los bebés que no pueden ser amamantados.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren hacer estudios más grandes en otros países para ver si el suplemento funciona igual en todas partes. También planean revisar si el suplemento afecta las alergias o el asma más adelante.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Añadir un suplemento probiótico con azúcares de leche materna a la fórmula ayuda a proteger a los bebés alimentados con fórmula contra infecciones respiratorias y mejora su salud inmunológica.
